title: Binary Search Bay
description: Halve the search space every step, on arrays and on answers.

challenges.prompt: Write classic binary search on a sorted array.
challenges.explanation: With hi = len − 1 (inclusive), the loop must run while lo <= hi. Using lo < hi skips the last remaining candidate, so a one-element array would never be checked.

challenges.prompt: What is the time complexity of binary search on n sorted items?
challenges.explanation: Each comparison throws away half of what is left.

challenges.prompt: Roughly how many comparisons does binary search need, at most, to search 1,000,000 sorted items?
challenges.explanation: 2²⁰ ≈ 1,048,576, so 20 halvings are enough. That is why log n feels almost constant.

challenges.prompt: What must be true for binary search to work?
options: The data is sorted, or the condition is monotonic
The size is a power of two
challenges.explanation: Binary search needs a yes/no question whose answer flips only once across the range. A sorted array is the most common example.

challenges.prompt: Find the minimum eating speed that lets Koko finish all banana piles within h hours. Which pattern?
options: Greedy: always eat the biggest pile
challenges.explanation: If speed s works, any faster speed works too. That monotonic yes/no lets you binary search the answer between 1 and the largest pile.

challenges.prompt: A sorted array was rotated, like [4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2]. Can you still find a target in O(log n)?
options: No, rotation forces a linear scan
Yes: at every mid, one half is still sorted, so you can tell which half to keep
Only if there are no negative numbers
challenges.explanation: Compare nums[mid] to the ends to see which half is in order, then check whether the target lies in that half.

challenges.prompt: Versions 1..n: once a version is bad, every later one is bad too. Find the first bad version with the fewest API calls.
options: Binary search for the leftmost bad version
challenges.explanation: The pattern is good, good, ..., bad, bad. Binary search for the boundary: if mid is bad, the answer is at mid or to its left.

challenges.prompt: Why do Java and C++ code often write mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2 instead of (lo + hi) / 2?
options: It rounds up instead of down
lo + hi can overflow a fixed-size integer
challenges.explanation: For very large indices, lo + hi can exceed the int limit and wrap negative. The subtraction form never exceeds hi.
